newsitem.title: GERMANY: German minister blames Britain for BSE crisis.
newsitem.headline: German minister blames Britain for BSE crisis.

text.p: Britain was mainly to blame for calamitous delays in fighting mad cow disease, Germany's farm minister, Jochen Borchert, was quoted on Saturday as saying.
He vowed in a newspaper interview that Germany would not make the same errors with the livestock scourge,

Borchert's criticism of Britain came as German state agriculture agencies tried to determine whether a German calf with bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) was born in Britain, as Borchert suspects, or in Germany as documents suggest.

The calf was the first discovery of BSE in Germany. The state agriculture ministry in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and state prosecutors said there was increasing evidence that the calf's earmarkings and documents had been manipulated.

Borchert told the Lausitzer Rundschau newspaper Germany would keep the public completely informed about BSE, adding that there would not be any "information deficit" here. He said Britain had mishandled the BSE crisis from an early stage.
"There was a failure to take the required actions in a timely fashion at the European level, but especially in Great Britain," Borchert said in the interview.

Arguing German cattle were completely safe, Borchert said he was dismayed that Poland, Hungary and Croatia had recently banned the import of German beef after it emerged last month that the calf, known as "Cindy", had BSE.
"There are no risks of BSE whatsoever from cattle originating in Germany," Borchert said.
State prosecutors in Neubrandenburg were investigating whether the calf "Cindy" that died in December had been wearing falsified earmarkings.

A cattle breeding association examiner in the northern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern said the calf's documents had been tampered with. Klaus Pfeiffer told NDR radio he had been reckless in failing to examine the animal's papers thoroughly.
"We just are not able to examine all the calves at birth," Pfeiffer said. "We have to handle 100 farms with more than 1,000 births each year."

Martin Brick, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern's agriculture minister, said that there was increasing evidence that "Cindy's" documents had been falsified and that the calf may have in fact been illegally imported from Britain.

Investigators have found, for example, that two other Galloway breed cows were wearing earmarks with the same identification number as "Cindy". The number on "Cindy" was also identical to a number for a calf named "Rita" that was imported from Britain, according to Borchert.
Authorities said they would conduct genetic tests on cows in Britain and in Germany to determine the calf's ancestry.

As many as 50,000 cattle in Germany may be slaughtered if it turns out the BSE calf descended from British stock. The agriculture ministry has already ordered the culling of more than 5,000 cattle imported from Britain and Switzerland and another 40,000 offspring may also be slaughtered.
